newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB set to weaken franc in worst-case EMU scenario.
newsitem.headline: SNB set to weaken franc in worst-case EMU scenario.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank does not expect Europe's single currency project to create excessive turbulence on foreign exchange markets, but is ready to use "unlimited" intervention to weaken the Swiss franc if need be, SNB board member Bruno Gehrig said.

In the text of an address to an economic seminar in Lucerne, Gehrig reiterated the SNB's stance that it will loosen monetary policy or even set an upper limit for the franc's exchange rate if speculative flows make the currency appreciate sharply.

"The crux of the matter is that the politically dictated timetable is proving to be very ambitious measured against progress on meeting the economic criteria" for Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU), he said.

"Most countries may well fall short of the fiscal criteria, which has the potential to be very sensitive politically," he said, adding it was difficult to estimate how financial markets that until now have viewed EMU benignly would react.
The risk profile for the euro currency will not be clear until it is determined if and when latecomers join the monetary union and under what conditions, he said.
Gehrig said he could not rule out the possibility that disappointed investors could pull funds out of the euro and switch them into the franc as a safe haven currency.

"I don't want to paint the worst possible picture. I hold the risk of an excessive impact on exchange rates as very small," he said, but added it was still wise to draw up potential responses to worst-case scenarios.

Using aviation and weather metaphors, Gehrig said that in the "not improbable" case that EMU prompts a mild storm, the SNB could cling to its money supply compass and let automatic stabilisers do their work.
"Experience of recent years has made clear, however, that this stabilising effect quickly reaches its limit," he said.

"If strong, steady rain sweeps the euro area, we cannot get around disregarding the compass and orientating ourselves by sight. We would have to loosen monetary policy further to have a certain compensation for the franc's strength," he said.
It would require courage to let money supply grow sharply, as it did in 1995 and 1996, he added, but said this was a risk the SNB would have to take if a strong franc was hurting the economy.
If gales continued to rock currency markets, then looser monetary policy alone may not suffice, Gehrig said.

"In such a scenario we would not get around showing the markets the way by setting a temporary exchange-rate upper limit and defending this upper limit with unlimited purchases of foreign exchange," he said.
"It is difficult to estimate how much extra liquidity would be required. In the interest of long-term stability we would have to remove it, not overnight but over a useful period," he said.
"There is no doubt that operating with an upper limit for exchange rates is a tricky manoeuvre for monetary policy. It can only come into consideration as a last resort."
The only other option would be to link the franc exchange rate to the euro, Gehrig said.
"One should never say never in a world of quick, often surprising change," he said, adding there were some conditions under which a permanent link might be a realistic option.
"But as long as the euro has not yet passed its performance test and not yet won the markets' trust, this variation cannot be considered," he said, adding the price would be too high.

Switzerland would lose its monetary policy autonomy, its ability to use exchange rates to cushion economic divergence with the EU and its interest rate bonus that keeps domestic rates 1.5 to 2.0 percent below levels in even the most stable countries, he noted.
